{{Short description|Prime-counting algorithm}}
The '''Meissel–Lehmer algorithm''' (after [[Ernst Meissel]] and [[Derrick Henry Lehmer]]) is an [[algorithm]] that computes exact values of the [[prime-counting function]].<ref name="lehmer" /><ref name="lagarias-miller-odlyzko" />

== Description ==

The problem of counting the exact number of primes less than or equal to ''x'', without actually listing them all, dates from [[Adrien-Marie Legendre | Legendre]]. He observed from the [[Sieve of Eratosthenes]] that
: <math>\pi (x) - \pi (x^{1/2}) + 1 = \lfloor x \rfloor - \sum_{i} \lfloor x/p_i \rfloor + \sum_{i<j} \lfloor x/p_ip_j \rfloor - \ldots</math>

where {{Math|{{floor|''x''}}}} is the [[Floor and ceiling functions | floor function]], which denotes the greatest [[integer]] less than or equal to {{Mvar|x}} and the {{Math|''p<sub>i</sub>''}} run over all primes {{Math|&leq; {{radic|''x''}}}}.<ref name="lehmer" /><ref name="lagarias-miller-odlyzko" />

Since the evaluation of this sum formula becomes more and more complex and confusing for large ''{{Mvar|x}}'', Meissel tried to simplify the counting of the numbers in the Sieve of Eratosthenes. He and Lehmer therefore introduced certain sieve functions, which are detailed below.

=== Key functions ===

Let {{Math|''p''<sub>1</sub>, ''p''<sub>2</sub>, &mldr;, ''p''<sub>''n''</sub>}} be the first {{Mvar|n}} primes. For a [[natural number]] {{Math|''a'' &geq; 1}}, define
: <math>\varphi(x, a) := \left| \left \{ n \le x : p|n \implies p > p_a \right \} \right|,</math>
which counts natural numbers no greater than ''{{Mvar|x}}'' with all prime factors greater than {{Math|''p''<sub>''a''</sub>}}. Also define for a natural number {{Mvar|k}},

: <math>P_k(x, a) := \left| \left \{ n \le x : n = q_1 q_2 \cdots q_k, ~\text{with}~ q_1, \ldots, q_k > p_a \right \} \right|,</math>

which counts natural numbers no greater than ''{{Mvar|x}}'' with exactly ''{{Mvar|k}}'' prime factors, all greater than {{Math|''p''<sub>''a''</sub>}}. With these, we have

:<math>\varphi(x, a) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty P_k(x, a),</math>

where the sum only has finitely many nonzero terms because {{Math|1=''P''<sub>''k''</sub>(''x'', ''a'') = 0}} when {{Math|''p''{{su|b=''a''|p=''k''}} > ''x''}}. Using the fact that {{Math|1=''P''<sub>0</sub>(''x'', ''a'') = 1}} and {{Math|1=''P''<sub>1</sub>(''x'', ''a'') = ''&pi;''(''x'') &minus; ''a''}}, we get

:<math>\pi(x) = \varphi(x,a) + a - 1 - \sum_{k=2}^\infty P_k(x,a),</math>

which proves that one may compute {{Math|''&pi;''(''x'')}} by computing {{Math|''&phi;''(''x'',''a'')}} and {{Math|''P''<sub>''k''</sub>(''x'', ''a'')}} for {{Math|''k'' &geq; 2}}. This is what the Meissel–Lehmer algorithm does.

=== Formula for ''P''<sub>''k''</sub>(''x'', ''a'') ===
For {{Math|1=''k'' = 2}}, we get the following formula for {{Math|''P''<sub>''k''</sub>(''x'', ''a'')}}:
:<math>\begin{align}
P_2(x, a) & =\left| \left\{ n : n \le x,~ n = p_b p_c, ~\text{with}~ a < b \le c \right\} \right| \\
& = \sum_{b = a+1}^{\pi(x^{1/2})} \left| \left\{ n : n \le x,~ n = p_b p_c, ~\text{with}~ b \le c \le \pi \left( \frac{x}{p_b} \right) \right\} \right| \\
& = \sum_{b = a+1}^{\pi(x^{1/2})} \left( \pi\left( \frac{x}{p_b} \right) - (b-1) \right) \\
& = \binom{a}{2} - \binom{\pi(x^{1/2})}{2} + \sum_{b = a+1}^{\pi(x^{1/2})} \pi\left( \frac{x}{p_b} \right).
\end{align}</math>
For {{Math|''k'' &geq; 3}}, the identities for {{Math|''P''<sub>''k''</sub>(''x'', ''a'')}} can be derived similarly.<ref name="lehmer" />

=== Expanding {{math|1=''&phi;''(''x'', ''a'')}} ===
With the starting condition 
: <math>\varphi(x, 0) = \lfloor x \rfloor,</math>
and the recurrence
: <math>\varphi(x, a) = \varphi(x, a-1) - \varphi\left(\frac x {p_a}, a-1 \right),</math>
each value for {{Math|''&phi;''(''x'',''a'')}} can be calculated recursively.

=== Combining the terms ===
The only thing that remains to be done is evaluating {{Math|''&phi;''(''x'',''a'')}} and {{Math|''P''<sub>''k''</sub>(''x'', ''a'')}} for {{Math|''k'' &geq; 2}}, for certain values of {{Mvar|x}} and {{Mvar|a}}. This can be done by direct sieving and using the above formulas.

== History ==

Meissel already found that for {{Math|''k'' &geq; 3}}, {{Math|1=''P''<sub>''k''</sub>(''x'', ''a'') = 0}} if {{Math|1=''a'' = ''&pi;''(''x''<sup>1/3</sup>)}}. He used the resulting equation for calculations of {{Math|''&pi;''(''x'')}} for big values of {{Mvar|x}}. <ref name="lehmer" />

Meissel calculated {{Math|''&pi;''(''x'')}} for values of ''{{Mvar|x}}'' up to {{Math|10<sup>9</sup>}}, but he narrowly missed the correct result for the biggest value of ''{{Mvar|x}}''.<ref name="lehmer" />

Using his method and an [[IBM 701]], Lehmer was able to compute the correct value of {{Math|''&pi;''(10<sup>9</sup>)}} and missed the correct value of {{Math|''&pi;''(10<sup>10</sup>)}} by 1.<ref name="lehmer" />

== Extended algorithm ==

[[Jeffrey Lagarias]], [[Victor S. Miller|Victor Miller]] and [[Andrew Odlyzko]] published a realisation of the algorithm which computes {{Math|''&pi;''(''x'')}} in time {{Math|''O''(''x''<sup>2/3+''&epsilon;''</sup>)}} and space {{Math|''O''(''x''<sup>1/3+''&epsilon;''</sup>)}} for any {{Math|''&epsilon;'' > 0}}.<ref name="lagarias-miller-odlyzko" /> Upon setting {{Math|1=''a'' = ''&pi;''(''x''<sup>1/3</sup>)}}, the tree of {{Math|''&phi;''(''x'',''a'')}} has {{Math|''O''(''x''<sup>2/3</sup>)}} leaf nodes.<ref name="lagarias-miller-odlyzko" />

This extended Meissel-Lehmer algorithm needs less computing time than the algorithm developed by Meissel and Lehmer, especially for big values of ''{{Mvar|x}}''.

Further improvements of the algorithm are given by M. Deleglise and J. Rivat in 1996 and X. Gourdon in 2001 (unpublished).<ref name="deleglise" /><ref name="Oliveira" />
